text: The Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 under natural criteria (ix) and (x).
The Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve was designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1996.
The archipelago was designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2014 (site 'Archipel Bolama-Bijagós').
Three marine protected areas — João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park, Orango Islands National Park and the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area — were created in 2000 and 2005.
UNESCO identifies the archipelago as the second most important foraging area in Africa for migratory waterbirds of the East Atlantic Flyway, and as a sanctuary for a diversity of sharks and rays.
UNESCO attributes the property's exceptional state of conservation mainly to how the area is organised and to traditional resource management by local communities.
Sacred islands governed by customary rules act as refuges for biodiversity.
Overall management of the World Heritage property is coordinated by the Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas (IBAP).

BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project aims to establish a community marine protected area on the islands of Unhocomo and Unhocomozinho, recognised as sanctuaries for juvenile sea turtles (proposal, not yet designated).
Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025 as a natural property (“Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô”).
Agriculture, forest use, animal husbandry, fishing, shell gathering and ecological tourism are the main activities of island communities.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Shellfish are the principal source of animal protein for island communities.
Tourism in the archipelago has developed over recent decades but remains limited.
Created in 2000, Orango National Park is a core area of the Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve and is classified as IUCN Category II.
The archipelago, notably Orango, hosts hippopotamuses that live in seawater on an almost permanent basis — according to UNESCO, the only place in the world where the species does so.
Five of the world's seven sea turtle species frequent the park's beaches.
The park is also home to several monkey species, African manatees and several reptile species.
The park includes 33 villages with an estimated 3,369 inhabitants, mainly of the Bijagó ethnic group.

The Rio Cacheu is not a river in the strict sense but a ria, where the sea reaches more than 150 km inland.
The region contains the Cacheu River mangroves, considered the largest continuous block of mangroves in West Africa.
Communities in and around the Cacheu park practise a sophisticated form of rice farming on mangrove soils, a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups (notably Felupe and Baiote).
Created in December 2000 by Decree-Law no. 12/2000 and managed by IBAP.
Wetland of International Importance (Ramsar site no. 2229) since 22 May 2015, with a listed area of 88,615 ha.
Its mangroves are considered the largest continuous mangrove block in West Africa; six mangrove species have been recorded.
The park's aims are to protect mangroves as the basis for fish reproduction, to conserve biodiversity and to improve living conditions of residents.
The mangroves provide food and refuge for protected or rare species such as the hippopotamus and the West African manatee, and serve as spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Each village in the site keeps one or more sacred forests, which act as reservoirs of biodiversity.

Besides rice fields, the mangrove provides fish, timber, honey, salt and traditional medicine.
Mangrove rice farming here is a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups and is described as unique cultural heritage.

Wetlands International reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.

Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2014 as a natural property (“Okavango Delta”).

Moremi Game Reserve (4,610 km²), the only part protected against all consumptive use, covers under a quarter of the property; the other three quarters are 18 Wildlife Management Areas and one Controlled Hunting Area. The Wildlife Management Areas are tribal land held in trust by the Tawana Land Board, which leases them to tourism operators or community trusts.
The Okavango Delta Management Plan 2021–2028 is the main management instrument, with the Department of National Museum and Monuments leading oversight and reporting to the World Heritage Committee.

In 2025 the World Heritage Committee encouraged Botswana to fully implement the management plan to address tourism pressure, pollution, water use, human–elephant conflict, wildfires and invasive species, and asked for an updated report by 1 December 2026.
Local communities fish, collect thatching grass, reeds, firewood and other veld products, practise flood-recession (molapo) farming, and run tourism in community concession areas.
The Ramsar sheet credits the Hambukushu as the original makers of Botswana's well-known baskets and the Bayei with bringing the mokoro (dug-out canoe) to the delta.

Community trusts such as the Khwai Development Trust (photographic tourism, three campsites) and the Mababe Zokotsama Development Trust (86 permanent staff in July 2023) earn income from tourism in their allocated areas.

Akanda National Park lies a few kilometres from Libreville on the Mondah and Corisco bays; its shore is dominated by about 35,000 ha of relatively undisturbed mangroves, mudflats and swamp forest, and its mudflats host 35,000–40,000 wintering Palearctic waders.

The park is managed by the Agence Nationale des Parcs Nationaux (ANPN); its Ramsar site shares the park's boundaries (54,000 ha), and the 2024 Ramsar sheet records its legal protection as only partly applied.
A 2023 study found that immature fish of several commercially important species dominate catches in the park's mangroves, confirming their role as a nursery for Mondah Bay fisheries.
Fishing is the most practised activity in and around the park, all year round; most people living along its edges are fishers, some professional and others, mainly local people, for subsistence.

The 2014–2018 management plan counted about 40 villages and parts of Libreville on the park's edge, with over 10,000 people outside the main towns, living mainly from fishing, farming, livestock, hunting and hand sawing of timber.
The Fang, Benga and Sekiani communities benefit from fishing, farming, hunting, tourism and recreation at the site.

The Angolan government signed a long-term management agreement for Iona with African Parks in December 2019 (with the environment ministry and the national biodiversity institute), and handover took place on 31 January 2020.
The 15,150 km² park lies at the northern tip of the Namib Desert between the Atlantic and the Curoca and Cunene rivers, and adjoins Namibia's Skeleton Coast National Park.
Decades of war wiped out species such as black rhino and elephant and drove local communities into Namibia; people returned after the conflict ended.
African Parks says some 7,000 people, including Himba, live within the park and on its immediate edge.

In a 2016 survey of 356 residents, 92% ranked livestock keeping as their most important activity, and maize was the most important crop; residents reported about 31,660 goats and 11,342 cattle in the park.
Iona received 6,102 visitors in 2025, 53% of them Angolan, many drawn by the dunes and by fishing.

Declared a protected area in 1983 (Decree No. 1068), the park lies at the southern tip of Sinai, about 12 km from Sharm El-Sheikh, and covers land and sea; reported areas differ between sources (460 km² to 850 km²).
The Nature Conservation Sector of the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA) is responsible for managing Egypt's protected areas, including Ras Mohammed.

In November 2018 it became the first marine protected area in Africa and the Middle East to receive IUCN Green List certification; monitoring cited by IUCN found average live coral cover above 65%, against 20–30% typical outside the reserve.
The local Bedouin community holds an exclusive tourism concession in the park; land-based tourism, some boat tours and all camping are managed by the Bedouin community under it.
The park has hired Bedouin as skippers and community guards, and a GEF/UNDP project built shaded pavilions where local Bedouin groups sell food and other products to visitors.
When COVID-19 halted park tourism in 2020, hundreds of local tourism workers such as guides, drivers and boat captains lost their jobs, and local women who make handicrafts lost their income.

Gorongosa was proclaimed a national park in 1960, and Gorongosa Mountain was added to the park in 2010.

The park is co-managed under a long-term public–private agreement between the Government of Mozambique and the Gorongosa Restoration Project (Carr Foundation), signed in 2008 for 20 years and later extended by 25 years.

Large-herbivore populations fell by more than 90% during the 1977–1992 civil war. Total biomass has largely recovered since, but the species mix has changed: elephant, hippo and buffalo now make up a much smaller share.
About 200,000 people live in the park's buffer zone, mostly subsistence farmers; many cultivate along the Pungue River on the park's southern boundary.
Coffee is grown on Gorongosa Mountain: of 1,056 farmers engaged in the park's programme, nearly 64% had productive plants, and household coffee income averaged about USD 400 from the 2024 harvest.
Between October 2024 and March 2025, the park's buffer-zone project reported over USD 451,000 from value chains: coffee, honey, cashew and ecotourism services.

Gazetted as a national park in 2007, Bwabwata (6,100 km²) is zoned into core conservation areas along the Okavango River in the west and the Kwando River in the east, with a multiple-use zone between them where people live.
Park residents formed the Kyaramacan Association in 2005 with IRDNC's help to manage and benefit from the park's resources; NACSO says it represents over 5,000 people, about 80% of them Khwe San.
MEFT holds legal authority over the park, and its management plan includes a land-use plan for the resident zone and foresees a formal co-management agreement with the Kyaramacan Association.

The management plan says residents' livelihoods depend almost entirely on the park's natural resources, apart from social grants and some jobs in the park; tceu, ‡ûmbé and /qom are the most important wild foods for most residents.
The Kyaramacan Association earns revenue from two trophy-hunting concessions (quotas worth about N$7.5 million in 2018) and from tourism, including the N//goabaca campsite at Popa Falls.
Devil's claw harvesting is an important income stream for residents; NACSO reports almost US$90,000 shared among 562 harvesters (317 women) in 2013, and a craft centre sells Khwe baskets.

Listed as “Parque Natural” by Assembleia Nacional, São Tomé e Príncipe (via FAOLEX); Government of São Tomé and Príncipe, submitted to the CBD.

Created by Law No. 6/2006, the park has three separate protection zones on São Tomé (the central-western mountain massif, Praia das Conchas–Lagoa Azul in the north and the Malanza mangrove in the south) and is surrounded by a buffer zone.

It covers 235 km² (27% of São Tomé); together with Príncipe's park it holds the country's most important tropical forests and significant populations of globally threatened endemic species, and there are no permanent communities inside the parks.
Internal regulations for the park were approved by Decree-Law No. 10/2025, and BirdLife International signed a memorandum with the government in 2017 to co-manage the protected areas.
About fifty communities live in the buffer zones, where farming cooperatives, especially for pepper, are active.
Residents around the park live mainly from subsistence farming and take timber for houses and boats, charcoal and non-timber products from nearby forests, including the park.
At Malanza a local group runs canoe trips in the mangrove, and an ecolodge and mangrove tours bring income to some community members; eco-guides of the Monte Pico Association depend on tourism.

The park was formally declared in 1995 and covers 822 km², including southern Mafia Island and the whole of Chole, Juani, Jibondo and Bwejuu islands; as many as 18,000 people live in villages at least partly inside its boundary.

It is managed through zoning: no human activity is permitted in core zones, fishing in specified-use zones is limited to park residents using legal gear, and general-use zones are open to fishers from Mafia District and beyond who hold a park permit. The park superintendent reports to the Marine Parks and Reserves Unit (MPRU).
Juani Island, which lies within the park, hosts the largest green turtle rookery on Mafia Island; the nesting female population was estimated at 41–72 for 2012–2018.
Jibondo Island, home to about 2,700 people inside the park, relies heavily on marine resources, trading and a long-standing boat-building tradition.
The park's reefs are heavily fished: surveyors in 2021 observed large numbers of fishers at several reefs, and fishing vessels that had come from Dar es Salaam.
SCUBA diving is a popular tourist activity within the park.

The park is managed by the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA). Research and monitoring are led by Mbarara University's Institute of Tropical Forest Conservation, and the Bwindi Mgahinga Conservation Trust supports community work outside the park.
Bwindi holds about half of the world's mountain gorillas; the 2018 census counted 459, up from 400 in 2011.
The 321 km² forest is an isolated island in one of Uganda's most densely populated rural areas. There is no buffer zone apart from a 4 km strip that communities donated at its southern end.
Gorilla tourism has grown from about 1,300 visitors a year in 1993 to 36,341 in 2019 and about 39,000 in 2023, with gorilla permits costing US$700.
Specialist resource users from forest-edge communities may harvest honey, medicinal plants and basketry materials in designated zones under negotiated agreements.
Smallholders near the park grow Arabica coffee alongside tea, bananas, cassava and maize; falling tea prices have led some farmers in Kanungu District to switch to coffee.

The 2025 milestone review found delays in the consent protocol and Indigenous Peoples Plan, said political challenges in the co-management set-up must be resolved soon, and judged community income opportunities still early and not yet at scale.
IUCN rates climate change as the immediate highest threat to the property, because warmer, drier conditions reduce inflows and the area and duration of flooding.

IUCN reports that up to 22% of the Cubango River's dry-season flow was lost between Katwitwi and the Cuito confluence in 2021 (16% in 2023), while small pumps drawing river water in Namibia rose from 25 to 130 between 2017 and 2023.
The same assessment reports that, with new commercial farms in Angola, irrigated land in the basin grew from 6,199 ha in 2020 to 8,025 ha in 2024, growth driven mostly by private operators.

In 2025 the World Heritage Committee noted with concern proposed upstream roads, dams and irrigation schemes in Angola and Namibia and asked that they undergo environmental impact assessment before any decision.
Botswana's 2024 report says human–elephant conflict persists in and around the property, and that heavy, repeated crop damage has led many farmers to abandon their fields.
Citing a 2021 Statistics Botswana pilot index, the report puts multidimensional poverty in the western Okavango Delta at 60.8% (10% extreme) and links its severity largely to human–elephant conflict.
During the management-plan review, communities reported that wild fruits they gather were no longer available because of competition from elephants and baboons.
The 2025 Committee decision encourages Botswana to expedite a comprehensive human–wildlife conflict strategy.

A Salvinia infestation first recorded in 2017 on the Xudum River had spread to Xigera Lagoon in Moremi Game Reserve by February 2025, and IUCN says the weed now occurs in almost half the delta's wetland extent.
Botswana reports that Salvinia blocks channels, lowers oxygen in the water, causes fish deaths and disrupts navigation, fishing and tourism.

IUCN also reports the invasive tree Ailanthus excelsa in all villages south and west of the delta, including Jedibe/Jao in the heart of the property, and calls for immediate eradication and monitoring.
IUCN finds local communities' role in decision-making still limited, particularly on resource access and tourism revenue-sharing.

According to IUCN, the Committee's request to expand programmes for traditional resource use, access rights and tourism participation has not been fully applied, and Indigenous Peoples still struggle to be allocated ancestral lands in the property, notably in the panhandle.
IUCN cites research (Datla et al. 2023) showing that delta communities are unhappy with constrained access and limited influence over water governance.
Visits rose from 77,550 in 1994/95 to 520,012 in 2009/10 and were 444,653 in 2018/19, mostly people who snorkel or dive on the reefs.

Citing earlier studies, a 2023 review reports that the six most-visited dive sites receive over 70,000 divers a year, and that broken corals were far more common at sites open to divers (8.2%) than at closed sites (0.6–1.2%).
The same review concludes that current management frameworks seem insufficient to cope with rising visitation.

The Green Sharm El Sheikh project rates as high the risk that protection of the marine protected areas near Sharm El-Sheikh, including Ras Mohamed, is undermined by tourism growth and fishing pressure.
Sharm El-Sheikh's development now runs along the shore from the park's northern edge to Nabq; hotel rooms grew from 515 in 1988 to 51,695 in 2016, and diving boats from 26 to about 300.
Illegal fishing and rising demand for seafood from Sharm El-Sheikh's residents and restaurants have affected several reef fisheries.
Policies of the institutions developing tourism occasionally clash with the park's conservation strategies.
Entrance and camping fees were significant sources of the park's budget and were lost when protected areas closed to visitors from March to June 2020.
The Green Sharm project's baseline puts the combined average annual budget of the three South Sinai protected areas (Ras Mohamed, Nabq and Abu Galum) at USD 75,000.
The project's 2023 environmental and social assessment states that total financing for the South Sinai protected-area system is still insufficient and that some areas face a serious shortage.
The 2024 Ramsar sheet rates housing and urban areas as a high-impact threat, increasing both in the site and around it, and describes Libreville's expansion as disorderly.

It also reports sand extraction at Malibé and Safala west of the site and laterite extraction to the south-west, and says the new Libreville airport and the Ntoum–Cap Santa Clara railway threaten a bird nesting area nearby.
The 2014 management plan, citing a 2010 atlas, recorded five dune-sand quarries in the buffer zone, and noted four oil-exploration permits covering the park with no extraction under way.

On 22 May 2026 Gabon's Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree described as setting a buffer zone of 1 km on land plus 500 m into the mangroves around Akanda; the communiqué's title named the Raponda Walker Arboretum instead, and the press asked for clarification.

The 2024 Ramsar sheet's narrative says overfishing linked to strong immigration (three camps of non-local fishers inside the site) and prohibited gear has sharply reduced fish stocks, and that trawlers entering the Corisco and Mondah bays threaten the ecosystem; its threat table nonetheless rates fishing as low impact.
The 2014 management plan records that about 550 mainly Nigerian fishers removed from the park in 2012 were only pushed outside its limits, without reducing their pressure on its fish.
The same plan lists park fishing bans (on mullet for Bambouchine, and on another species for villages on the Ntoum–Cocobeach road) among the conflicts with local communities.
Because the park's mangroves are a nursery for juvenile commercial fish, their protection matters for keeping fisheries sustainable.
Over-exploitation of mangroves, especially for wood, is named among the site's chief threats.
The 2024 Ramsar sheet calls harvesting of plants for building wood and firewood, especially mangrove, a real threat to the site's ecosystems.
In the buffer zone, closing sand quarries and banning sawing and charcoal making in the villages of Malibé 1 and 2 caused considerable job losses, according to the 2014 management plan.
The 2024 Ramsar sheet says tourism inside the site is not yet organised, supervised or channelled under clear ecological principles.
In 2014 two operators (Mondah Ecotour and Cap Caravane) offered accommodation and visits in the park and buffer zone without any tourism concession agreement with ANPN.
Uncontrolled tourism within the site is listed among its chief threats.

Forest on Gorongosa Mountain shrank from more than 13,000 ha in 1977 to under 6,300 ha in 2023, leaving less than 47% of the original cover. Since 2010 about 411 ha a year has been lost, mostly to slash-and-burn agriculture.
The remaining forest is increasingly fragmented: average patch size fell from 15.1 ha in 1977 to 2.3 ha in 2023, and the largest continuous block from about 11,300 ha to about 1,900 ha.

The mountain's forests release rainwater that sustains downstream ecosystems and the livelihoods of thousands of people. New landslide and erosion scars covering about 20 ha appeared by 2023, which the park's scientists say may signal the ecosystem beginning to fail.
A 2012–2016 lion study found that by-catch in wire snares and steel-jaw traps set by bushmeat hunters was the main human factor limiting the lion population's recovery.

Snaring remained frequent through 2014, especially in outlying parts of the park; rangers confiscated 12,363 snares and 317 steel-jaw traps in 2015–2016, and after law enforcement was restructured, preliminary data showed snaring pressure falling by 49% between 2016 and 2017.
Snaring persists: in the first quarter of 2025 alone, the park's law enforcement team confiscated 552 wire snares and 28 gin traps.

As wildlife recovers inside the unfenced park, animals stray into neighbouring communities; the co-manager uses beehive fences to keep elephants out of crop fields and predator-proof bomas against livestock losses to lions and hyenas.
Elephants recovering from wartime losses raid crops along the park's southern boundary; two farmers were killed by crop-raiding elephants while a study of this behaviour was under way.
A field experiment using GPS-collared elephants tracked elephants leaving the park to raid crops outside it, and tested community-based fences (beehive, chili and combined) to reduce these crossings.
The management plan lists illegal settlement from the west and rising farming and cattle numbers among the park's greatest threats, and sets the target of removing all cattle.
Its foreword warns that gradual encroachment is a very high risk, that opportunistic people have started to occupy the park, and that access control must improve significantly.

The plan records that after cattle were removed in 1996, Hambukushu settlers brought in relatively large numbers of cattle; removing all cattle, as a 1999 Cabinet decision required for the north-east parks, is still described as essential and not to be postponed.

In October 2021 the Mbukushu Traditional Authority submitted a petition seeking to set aside the park's national-park status, mainly to lift restrictions on land use and cattle farming; a parliamentary committee planned a fact-finding visit for March 2022.
Snapshots of the late dry seasons of 2014 and 2019 showed 11 and 16 active fires burning in the park at one time, which the management plan calls extraordinary for a Namibian national park.
Intense late fires have visibly thinned deciduous woodlands, especially in the west, and reduced fire-sensitive trees such as Pterocarpus angolensis.
The early-burning target (up to 50% of the park) has not been met: in only 3 of 17 years did more than 20% burn in the early dry season.
The plan links better fire management to more wild food in the resident zone, and so to residents' food security.
MEFT's poaching database records 60 elephants illegally killed in Bwabwata in 2016, falling to 45, 12 and 7 in 2017–2019.
The plan nevertheless judges the risk of illegal killing still high, names elephant poaching a high priority, and notes poachers from Botswana crossing the park.

The Legal Assistance Centre says the Khwe can take part in decisions on resources and trophy-hunting benefits only through the Kyaramacan Association, which is not exclusively Khwe, and that the state recognised the Mbukushu but not a Khwe traditional authority.

In July 2024 Khwe residents petitioned for recognition of their own chief, citing villages facing water scarcity, without grid electricity or jobs; a ministerial approval of a Khwe Traditional Authority had been put on hold after the Hambukushu Traditional Authority objected.
The management plan notes that the Kyaramacan Association has experienced governance problems and calls for renewed joint management with MEFT.

In February 2022 a member of parliament gave notice of questions alleging that the Association's bank signatories included ministry directors and that the community had no signing powers, and demanded an audited financial report.
Parts of the park's buffer zone have been used by intensive agricultural companies (Agripalma, SATOCAO).

The park's 2021–2025 management plan, as reproduced in a 2025 thesis, records that Agripalma (Socfin) was granted 4,917 ha and cleared forest from the south of the island up to the park boundary between 2009 and 2013.
The same plan reports market gardening at Bom Sucesso expanding significantly into the park, with clearing that causes erosion and frequent pesticide use.
BirdLife reports that buffer-zone forests meant to stay free of development have been threatened by plans for industrial oil palm and a hydroelectric dam.
In 2020 BirdLife reported a significant increase in illegal logging for construction and backed a plan to build five surveillance posts on the main timber-trafficking routes.

The park plan notes selective felling for building (80% of houses are wooden), including on the roadless south-west coast where timber leaves by boat, and that about 75% of the population uses firewood or charcoal.
At the Praia das Conchas mangrove, cutting of mangrove trees for charcoal has had a considerable impact, and waste from the Lobata dump upstream is an aggravating factor.

A 2019 check of the Malanza mangrove boundary could not find a number of the 2015 boundary marks, probably because the trees bearing them were cut, and found three critical areas of encroachment, mainly tree felling and farming.
The island's forests hold three critically endangered endemic birds; nearly all the most important forests are in the park, and the Dwarf Ibis is directly affected by illegal hunting.

Island-wide, BirdLife reported in 2026 that the Dwarf Ibis is believed to number fewer than 2,000 and the São Tomé Grosbeak and Newton's Fiscal fewer than 250 each, under pressure from hunting, disturbance, invasive mammals and habitat loss; as most of their key forest lies in the park, these pressures bear largely on it.
The park plan records that uncontrolled hunting and capture of endemic and threatened species persist in the park, and that palm-wine tapping is degrading some areas even in its core.

Effective protection since 2006 has been hampered by limited staff, funding and enforcement capacity, including poor boundary marking and little visible staff presence; the 2015–2020 management plans were held back by lack of funds.
The park's ability to apply protection measures is limited, and enforcement responsibilities are unclear between the park, coast guard, police, forest directorate and district council.

Scarce resources have concentrated most work in the park's central zone, leaving its two mangrove areas largely without concrete conservation measures; their 2015 plans were only very partly implemented.

A 2021 survey found fishers using the park's reefs regardless of zoning, after a government directive linked to the 2020 general election allowed fishers free access; park staff reported they could not enforce park regulations at the time.
Kitutia, a no-take core zone close to Jibondo village where fishers using modified (illegal) seine nets are based, had the lowest fish biomass of the five reefs surveyed in 2021.
In June 2022 the MPRU survey team saw pull-net fishing on the way to Mange Reef and described it as the most unsustainable destructive practice still found in the park.

Both monitoring reports describe the park's 2006 regulations as too weak to deter illegal fishing; the 2021 report notes that a beach-seine offence inside the park carried a TSh 20,000 fine, against TSh 500,000 or more under national fisheries rules outside it.
In 2021, small non-target fish dominated all five surveyed reefs, and predatory species such as groupers were seen mostly as juveniles, which the authors read as a sign of intensive fishing.

In the 2022 grouper baseline, every grouper recorded fell in the four smallest size classes and none exceeded 40 cm; the report concludes that fish communities are depleted throughout the park and that commercially important species are overfished.

Several of the park's monitored reefs were severely affected by a 2020 bleaching event, and overall rubble cover increased between 2018 and 2022, which MPRU attributes mainly to unsustainable fishing and anchoring by tourist boats.

Kitutia Reef, Jibondo's main fishing area, was hit by bleaching in 1998 and 2024, Cyclone Hidaya in 2024 and destructive fishing; some degraded sections have not recovered since 1998 because unstable rubble and algae prevent coral settlement.
Reefs exposed to seasonal Rufiji River floodwater (Mange and Nyamalile) had the highest macroalgae cover in 2022.
The Jibondo community went through about a decade of deep antagonism towards the park authority, and unemployment is a growing problem on the park's small islands.

Earlier alternative-livelihood programmes in the park (beekeeping, seaweed farming, handicrafts) produced low returns and did not replace fishing, and residents have viewed the sharing of park revenue as non-transparent.
MPRU recommends stronger stakeholder engagement and co-management to make up for park staff shortages and to build community ownership of the park.

Crop damage by elephants, gorillas, chimpanzees, baboons, bushpigs and other animals is still a source of conflict with farmers, and IUCN calls it the biggest threat to the improved relationship between people and the park.

The conflict is worsened by the park's long boundary and high population pressure along it. Crop raiding turns attitudes against conservation, reduces household food supply and is linked to poaching and snaring.

Mitigation has had patchy results because of limited funds for materials and weak farmer commitment to maintenance; 134 human–gorilla conflict (HUGO) volunteers cover frontline parishes, and a 4.1 km elephant hotspot is targeted for bee fences.
Hunting with wire snares and dogs continues, especially in remote areas and the frontline zone of the park, driven by poverty.
When tourism stopped during the COVID-19 closure, poaching increased. On 1 June 2020, a hungry community member hunting duiker and bushpig killed a habituated silverback gorilla.
Rangers removed 151 snares in May 2020, against 9 in May 2019, falling to 33 by October 2020.
The unsurfaced Ruhija road crosses the park's highest reaches and the narrow 'neck' joining its two parts; it appears to act as a barrier to gorilla movement, and there are proposals to pave it.

In April 2021 IGCP reported that construction of the Nteko–Buhoma road through the western park, linking Kisoro and Kanungu districts, had recently been launched; it said the road would significantly affect connectivity with the Sarambwe Nature Reserve in DR Congo and called for a robust environmental and social impact assessment.

As of April 2022 the planned surfaced road would cut about 3 km through the park, UWA had opposed both road projects, consultations were still under way and construction was not expected to start soon.

Community resentment of park management has been linked to the lack of support for crop losses and to inequity in how revenue-sharing benefits are distributed. The scheme passes 20% of gate fees and part of gorilla permit revenue to community projects (about US$1.18 million in 2018/19).

The Batwa were forcibly removed from the forest when the park was created. A Vulnerable and Marginalized Groups Plan (2020–2026) names unequal benefits, land access, livelihoods and limited participation in management as key challenges for them.
The 2020 closure showed how far community projects depend on tourism revenue, and IUCN calls for more diverse livelihood options.
Wetlands International introduced solar salt production on Dapack island (Cacheu) to replace boiling seawater with mangrove fuelwood.
The Restoration Initiative trained women on Elia Island in solar salt production, a less exhausting method that does not require cutting mangrove wood.
Elsewhere in Guinea-Bissau's coastal zone (Oio region), the DEDURAM project has offered women salt producers a solar technique since 2016.
Because the technique has already been introduced locally, a women-led solar salt enterprise is a plausible way to generate income while directly reducing fuelwood demand on mangroves.
In the village of Plindan (Cacheu), a fuelwood-efficient oven was installed to reduce fuelwood use for fish smoking, alongside a new women's association.
In the Bijagós, mangrove wood is used for smoking fish.
An earlier GEF-supported protected-areas project funded income-generating activities such as fish processing.
A fish-processing micro-enterprise built around fuel-efficient ovens could add value to artisanal catches while reducing mangrove cutting.
Women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River, have been trained in growing oysters by The Restoration Initiative.
The park's dense mangroves are spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Oyster cultivation creates income that depends on healthy mangroves, which could give communities a direct economic interest in protecting them.
Honey is among the services the Cacheu mangroves provide.

Wetlands International reports that the savings and loans groups it has set up in Guinea-Bissau since 2015 lend for activities including beekeeping, and describes a local beekeeper's mangrove-honey initiative (location within the country not stated).

A news report places beekeeping support within Wetlands International's project around the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, describing hives as 'mangrove guardians' because no one cuts a tree with an active hive.
A traceable mangrove-honey product could reward communities for keeping mangroves standing. Its commercial viability is unknown.
From 2015 to 2018, Wetlands International, IBAP and partners restored abandoned rice fields by breaching embankments and digging small channels to restore tidal flow.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Global Mangrove Watch publishes open mangrove-extent time series (CC BY 4.0) that could support baseline monitoring.
Results-based finance (e.g. carbon or biodiversity outcomes) for community-led restoration of abandoned rice fields could be explored, building on — not duplicating — the existing REDD+ project.
Ecological tourism is already one of the main activities of island communities.
A community guest house in Anôr village serves visitors to Orango.
Sacred forests are described as threatened by exploitative tourism.
Tourism that is community-owned and respects customary rules could add income while steering away from the exploitative forms identified as a threat.
The Urok community MPA is managed directly by local communities and aims to secure their access to prime fishing grounds.
BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project targets sustainable marine resource management and improved livelihoods in the archipelago's MPAs.
Traceable products from community-managed grounds (for example processed shellfish or fish) could link conservation outcomes to income, if harvest limits are respected.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Cashew expansion is reducing the preponderance of palm and rice.
Adding value to products from existing natural palm groves could make traditional agroforestry more competitive with cashew expansion.

IUCN NL and Eco-Benin are working to preserve mangroves in the Bouche du Roy reserve and surroundings, financed by blue carbon credits; planned work includes nurseries, village-led planting and alternative income, especially for women.
Eco-Benin reports more than 500 hectares planted and areas made sacred through traditional sacralisation practices in the Bouche du Roy (self-reported).
Community-run mangrove nurseries and paid restoration work are a plausible regenerative activity here, because an existing blue-carbon project already plans nurseries and alternative income.
UNESCO reports that since the reserve was created, projects have promoted ecotourism, particularly whale and dolphin watching.
The EU-funded AGeReB action (2023–2027), run by IUCN, IUCN NL and Eco-Benin, includes support for the Nonvignon tourism training centre.
Locally owned guiding and ecotourism services could offer income that depends on a healthy delta, as an alternative to resource overuse.
HYPREP's 'Mangrove Vanguards' programme trains young people and women to run mangrove nurseries, and requires restoration contractors to buy their seedlings.
HYPREP reports completing a first phase of mangrove restoration covering 560 ha and starting a second phase of 438 ha across seven communities (self-reported).
Because restoration contractors already buy community-grown seedlings, nursery enterprises are a defensible regenerative activity here, if demand continues beyond the current phases.
The 2013 Ramsar information sheet reports that more than 70 women derived their livelihood from salt extraction, an activity it describes as sustainable.
In 2012 the women's salt cooperative produced little salt and lost its traditional market, according to the grantee report.
Livestock faeces contaminate the salt collected for sale.
Keeping livestock out of the salt pans and marketing a cleaner, traceable traditional salt could strengthen the women's income while keeping the site in use. Market demand is unknown.

In October 2020 the national parks office (OIPR) and the World Bank-financed WACA project signed an agreement to develop and restore mangrove ecosystems in the Azagny and Îles Ehotilé parks (news report).
A local management committee coordinated by OIPR promotes participatory management with the park's neighbouring communities.
Community-run nurseries and paid restoration work could build on this agreement and on the existing local committee, if restoration funding continues.
Locally, men supply mangrove firewood and women smoke the fish.
In Guinea-Bissau, a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven was installed in Plindan (Cacheu) to reduce fuelwood use.
Fuel-efficient ovens run by women processors could reduce mangrove wood demand here too. No such initiative was found for this site.

A Rocha Ghana, with the Wildlife Division, reports planting 20 ha of degraded mangrove, establishing a woodlot and training community trainers in sustainable mangrove harvesting in four communities (2021–2023, self-reported).
The management plan describes a traditional cycle of planting and harvesting mangroves along the lower Volta creeks at Anyanui.
The Wildlife Division has established a tree nursery that distributes seedlings to surrounding communities.
Managed mangrove woodlots supplying fish-smoking fuelwood could relieve pressure on natural stands, building on local practice and recent project work.
The Wildlife Division is trying to promote bird watching and night turtle walks.
Community guiding services could share in this tourism and give residents an income linked to protecting nesting beaches and bird areas.
A 2025 CTCN technical-assistance plan, requested by a women fish traders' group at Togokomé, proposes replanting mangroves and solar fish smoking and cold storage (planned, not yet implemented).
The World Bank reports that 257 hectares of mangroves have been planted in Togo under the WACA programme.
Because women fish traders still cut mangroves for fuel, combining replanting with solar fish preservation addresses a documented cause of loss.
Since 2000 IUCN, the park, IFAD and FIBA have supported Imraguen women with processing facilities, hygiene and management training and new packaging for traditional products.
Inside the park only the Imraguen may fish, on foot or from sailing boats; motorised boats are banned.
Traceable traditional products tied to sail-only fishing could raise income per catch rather than catch volume, in line with the park's fishing rules.
UNESCO reports that grass-roots village associations run mangrove nurseries and reforestation plots.
A women's group in the delta has led mangrove reforestation since 2007 and set harvesting periods and biological rest periods (news report).
FAO reports training women seafood processors at Niodior in food safety, hygiene and entrepreneurship.
Women-led shellfish processing tied to harvest rules and mangrove replanting builds on documented local practice.
The Bamboung bolon became a community marine protected area in 2003, proposed and led by the Senegalese NGO Océanium with funding from the French Global Environment Facility.
IRD monitored its fish populations between 2003 and 2012.
Products or services linked to community-managed fishing areas could reward their protection. Viability and current status are unknown.
The Gambia designated the TRY Association with exclusive use rights to the cockle and oyster fishery in the Tanbi special management area.
TRY members agreed to extend the closed season to nine months to let oysters grow bigger.
A 2010 grant set up microcredit for members, who learned to pickle oysters for sale during the closed season.
TRY received a GEF grant through the National Environment Agency for mangrove reforestation and aquaculture.
Value-added oyster products sold under existing co-management rights could raise income without increasing harvest.
Guinée Écologie reports supporting ten women's groups with solar tarpaulins and technical help in the Konkouré delta and the Mélakoré estuary in 2025.
BirdLife reports a CEPF-funded pilot in Dubréka prefecture producing salt with sunlight and tarpaulins instead of fuelwood.
Since salt boiling is a documented driver of mangrove cutting here, women-led solar salt production is a defensible regenerative activity.
Guinée Écologie reports supporting 98 women in the Konkouré delta in 2025 to rebuild and use improved fish-smoking ovens.
Wider use of improved ovens could cut the fuelwood demand that drives mangrove cutting here.
Guinée Écologie installed oyster garlands at pilot sites, two of them in the Konkouré delta, in 2025.
PROMAK describes honey as a little-developed value chain in the Konkouré landscape, with a few pilot initiatives, and commissioned a 2026 market and value-chain study.
Oyster and honey products depend on healthy mangroves, so value chains built around them could reward protection, subject to the planned market study.
Freetown City Council reports planting 275,000 mangroves in three coastal communities, tracked digitally by community youth; whether these sites lie in the Ramsar site is not established.
A blue-carbon developer announced in May 2024 a conservation and restoration project covering 10,000 hectares of the estuary; its current status is unknown.
Community nurseries and paid planting could supply restoration in the estuary, if a restoration or carbon project proceeds.
In December 2024 the Sierra Leone Nature Guide Association trained stakeholders, youths and pupils around the Targreen wetland, part of the estuary, in bird conservation.
Trained local guides could offer birdwatching services that give residents an income linked to protecting bird habitat.
Wetlands International Africa supported the production and use of improved stoves with women in Fallie and Senbehun, and a cassava processing unit in Teh, under an EU-funded mangrove project (2025).
The 2007 Ramsar sheet records earlier trials of fish-smoking structures and a solar fish drier.
Locally made improved stoves and smokers could reduce demand for mangrove wood, the main fuel for fish smoking here.
A 2016–2017 small grant trained fishers in selective fishing, supplied approved net sizes and started cage fish farming on the lake (marked completed; no outcome data).
Legal-mesh fishing combined with small-scale fish farming could reduce pressure on juvenile fish while sustaining income.

A Community Artcraft Association formed in 2023 sells its members' work at local tourism fairs and events, and the Ovakande Homahere Sour Milk Association of ten Ovahimba women has been trained in governance, financial literacy and project management.
A community agricultural association in Monte Negro was set up through a partnership with FAO and receives training and basic farming materials.

The 2025 milestone review judged the park's initial steps towards community value chains early and not yet at scale, and recommended expanding livelihood and value-chain initiatives, including tourism, with Indigenous communities.

Turning these groups into steady small enterprises, for example by selling crafts and dairy products to the park's growing number of visitors, could diversify household income in an economy that relies heavily on livestock.
Visitor numbers are rising (6,102 in 2025, mostly Angolan), drawn by the dunes and fishing.

INBAC names Salojamba, Ponte Albina, Espinheira and Pediva as the busiest visitor points, with safari, camping and water-based outings as the main activities, and says tourism still needs funding, guides, camps and lodges.
The 2024 study suggests ecotourism could create incentives for community-based conservation, but notes that residents' views of tourism differ sharply by locality.
Guiding, campsite or cultural services run by residents at these visitor points might channel tourism income to communities; no such enterprise is documented yet.
Most enclosures in the park are built from bushes, and the study's authors note that the temporary enclosures of semi-nomadic herders are often easy for carnivores to get into.
Livestock predation is the main focus of the park's human–wildlife conflict work.
Sturdier, possibly mobile, enclosures built and maintained by trained local workers could cut losses and reduce reasons to poison leopard and cheetah, while creating some paid work.
The government controls Salvinia with a host-specific weevil (Cyrtobagous salviniae), now its preferred method, and reports partnerships with community groups and the private sector to widen control.
Botswana's 2022 report proposed rearing weevils at some safari operators and community trusts under a memorandum of understanding that includes training camp staff and trusts.
IUCN notes that tour guides in the core area have been trained to monitor Salvinia and that weevil breeding pools exist, but calls for a more coordinated and better-resourced response.
A trust-run rearing and monitoring service, paid by government or lodges, could turn an existing control method into local paid work while helping to scale up the response.

In 2015 Ecoexist reported hosting conservation-agriculture workshops and said over 40 panhandle farmers were using the techniques; the aim is higher yields on smaller plots that are easier to guard from elephants, alongside research on early planting and elephant-resistant crops.
Ecoexist also set out plans for an 'elephant economy' in the panhandle based on elephant-branded tourism, food and handicraft products.

Through OKACOM, the State Party supported six farmers at Shakawe with climate-smart conservation agriculture and 19 vegetable gardens along the Thamalakane River; IUCN notes that OKACOM-funded shallow irrigation wells dried out when groundwater fell.

Combining elephant-aware cropping with elephant-friendly branded products could cut crop losses and diversify income for buffer-zone farmers, building on conservation-agriculture work already tried locally and on Ecoexist's 2015 product plans.

The Khwai trust runs photographic tourism and three campsites, and the Mababe trust runs hunting tourism, campsites and a lodge; they employ residents directly or, at Khwai, also through joint-venture partners.
Botswana reports that income from community trusts in the property pays for community services such as funeral cover, school transport, household water connections and solar power for a school.
IUCN counts 14 community trusts in the panhandle but finds community influence over tourism revenue-sharing still limited.
Helping more trusts, especially in the panhandle, to own and run their own tourism products could spread benefits beyond the few established trusts, in areas where poverty is high.
Bedouin already run land tourism, some boat tours and all camping in the park under an exclusive concession.
A GEF/UNDP project built pavilions at Ras Mohammed where Bedouin groups sell food and other products.
Visitors surveyed in an earlier study preferred less crowded sites in exchange for healthier reefs, and its scenario with 50% fewer visitors gave a higher net benefit than the status quo.
Growing Bedouin-run guided, camping, food and craft services that earn more per visitor could add local income and park revenue without adding more people to the reefs.
Workshops and training have been organised for hotel staff, dive instructors and guides, and the park's rules distributed in several languages.
An earlier study at the park found that one briefing cut divers' contact with living coral from 0.9 to 0.15 times per diver per 7 minutes.

The Green Sharm project plans to identify best practices for Ras Mohamed and the other Sharm El-Sheikh protected areas (anchoring systems, carrying-capacity assessments, zoning) and to develop guidelines for diving and visits.
A local service that trains guides and gives standard briefings and in-water checks for operators could help these rules be followed at busy sites.
In 2014 Mondah Ecotour ran pirogue trips and walks in the park's mangroves and on botanical trails, without a concession agreement.
Local people have high expectations of the park, and tourism is often cited for its economic benefits.
Being close to Libreville gives the park a potentially leading role in environmental education, tourism and nearby recreation.
AFD's 2012–2018 project with ANPN aimed, among other goals, to promote the economic use of the Akanda and Pongara parks and public understanding of them.
Licensed tours run with local guides, under ANPN rules on routes, visitor numbers and fees, could turn unorganised tourism into income for people who now cut wood or fish in the park.

The park's mangroves are a nursery for commercial fish; the study's authors propose using such data for management plans, zoning and monitoring that take account of customary management and local knowledge.
Fishers' groups around the park are informal and organised village by village, and a local consultative management committee was planned for early 2014.
A coastal fisheries management project run by the fisheries directorate has been set up at the site but is still at an early stage.
A park-led World Wetlands Day event discussed traditional knowledge of artisanal fishing and sustainable fishing techniques with nearby communities.
Formalising local fishers' associations around agreed zones and legal gear could ease conflict over fishing bans and help control prohibited gear and outside fishing camps.
Better prices for legally caught fish (for example through shared cold storage or direct sales in Libreville) might make the rules easier to accept.

Coffee plantations under indigenous shade trees are visible on 2023 satellite imagery, with more woody cover than before the coffee project; the park's forest report says this land use should be expanded to counter deforestation, alongside reforestation and campaigns against forest clearing.
1,056 farmers are engaged in Gorongosa Mountain coffee; ten top performers earned more than USD 1,000 each from the 2024 harvest.

A new coffee processing plant, whose inauguration was reported in December 2025, is part of a EUR 20 million sustainable livelihoods programme funded by the Netherlands and run by the Gorongosa Restoration Project with Right to Play and Resilience.
In 2021 the park's science department began a 5-ha agroforestry restoration plot on the mountain, planting nearly 3,000 trees of nine native species with local communities.

With production, processing and market access already in place, local enterprises along the chain (native shade-tree nurseries, specialty processing, origin-branded sales) could raise farmers' returns from tree-covered plots and make them a stronger alternative to slash-and-burn.

Around Gorongosa, beehive fences placed at key crossing points cut the odds of elephants leaving the park by up to 95%, the most effective strategy tested, and also created opportunities for honey income.
The Gorongosa Project reports training 135 beekeepers through 17 lead beekeepers, distributing 666 hives and installing beehive fences in dozens of locations.
Honey contributed about USD 10,300 to buffer-zone value-chain income between October 2024 and March 2025.
Organising fence-line beekeepers into producer groups with shared processing and marketing could make fence maintenance pay for itself while reducing crop losses.
Kyaramacan Association members harvest devil's claw collectively under permits after training, refilling holes and leaving the mother root so the plant regrows.

FAO's Sustainable Wildlife Management Programme works with the Association, WWF Namibia and neighbouring conservancies on legal, sustainable harvesting, including resource surveys, quotas and fair buyer contracts.
NACSO describes the Association's devil's claw as organically certified and in demand, and the management plan lists it among conservation-related incomes to develop.

Strengthening this established, certified chain (for example local drying, grading and transparent payment records) could raise and spread residents' income while addressing concerns about how benefits are shared.
The plan's fire programme depends on early-dry-season burning and requires a collaborative approach with residents that draws on Khwe traditional knowledge of fire.
Before 2016, MEFT and residents cooperated on fire management, game counts and anti-poaching, and the Association employs its own game guards and resource monitors.
The plan says responding to many simultaneous late fires would be physically very challenging for the park's available staff, and the early-burning target is rarely met.
Contracting resident teams through the Association for early burning and fire response could help meet the target, protect wild-food woodlands and create local jobs.

The plan proposes a Kyaramacan Traditional Knowledge Centre offering Khwe cultural experiences, tracking and conservation courses, crafts sales, and a botanical garden with a nursery selling plants; a feasibility study is still required.
It also cites a survey in which 76% of residents interviewed cultivated wild-food plants, and recommends exploring this for food security and to ease harvesting pressure in core areas.
A craft centre near the eastern entrance of the multiple-use area already sells Khwe baskets.
A resident-run centre combining a wild-food nursery, crafts and cultural tourism could add income that rests on Khwe knowledge.

Eco-guides of the Monte Pico Association maintained the park's trails with BirdLife support in 2020, when BirdLife was also working to retrain 15 eco-guides for surveillance, awareness and monitoring of the park.

Since 2021, forest directorate agents and civil-society groups including the Monte Pico Association and a responsible-tourism platform have monitored biodiversity and threats in the parks twice a year.
At Malanza a community group already runs canoe tours in the mangrove.
Ecotourism is not yet advanced enough to bring significant benefits to local communities.
Combining paid guiding with paid monitoring could give local guides steadier income while adding a regular presence on trails and timber routes where staff are scarce.

In a 2022–2024 initiative on São Tomé, 75 hunters joined as 'Agents of Change' who help find rare birds and report illegal hunting; 25 were mentored on alternative activities and five business ideas received support.
In February 2023 more than 30 hunters, former hunters and officials were trained on hunting regulation to protect endemic species.
The critically endangered birds depend on forests that lie mostly within the park.
Extending support for hunters' alternative businesses, and paying former hunters to find birds for monitoring or birdwatching visits, could reduce hunting pressure in the park.
Demand from birdwatchers for the three critically endangered endemics might support guide fees.
Farming cooperatives, especially for pepper, are active in the buffer zones and contribute to their sustainable management.
Residents around the park depend mainly on subsistence farming, and market gardening at Bom Sucesso is spreading into the park.
Helping cooperatives earn more from shade crops on existing buffer-zone farmland could raise incomes without new clearing at the park edge.
Premium or certified markets for shade-grown pepper or cocoa might fund this.
MPRU recommends coral reef restoration in the park, with emphasis on bleaching-resistant coral genera.

A CEPF-funded project by The Ropes of Hope (2025–2026) plans coral nurseries and outplanting on Kitutia Reef and expects to train and employ up to 14 coral gardeners from Jibondo, with the Jibondo Village Council's agreement.
The grant document says the training could lead to later work in dive tourism, and notes earlier restoration trials at Shungimbili, Chole and Utumbi reefs.

Because a trained local workforce and active dive tourism already exist in the park, a community-run reef restoration and monitoring service paid by tourism operators or conservation funders could keep restoration jobs going after the grant ends.

In June 2024 a full assembly of Jibondo's voting-age adults unanimously supported restoring Kitutia Reef; the project's 1.1-hectare fishery replenishment zone, closed to all extraction, is to be formalised by the Jibondo Village Council with the park authority.

At Songo Songo, south-west of Mafia, community temporary reef closures for octopus, which WWF supports with awareness raising and training for the village Beach Management Unit, produced a catch of 37 tonnes in three days at the fourth reopening; people from Mafia have made study visits there, and WWF said it would raise funds to extend its piloted Songo Songo project (an ice-making cooling hub for the octopus catch) to areas such as Mafia.

Closures that fishers agree to and whose reopenings they share in could give park fishers a direct income reason to respect no-take areas, which top-down enforcement in the park has struggled to secure.

Conservation Through Public Health (CTPH) set up Gorilla Conservation Coffee because coffee farmers around Bwindi were not paid a fair price, which pushed them to rely on the park for food and fuelwood. It pays above-market prices and provides training and shade trees.
The enterprise started in 2015 with just over 100 farmers and reports working with 630 (230 of them women), having bought more than 100 tonnes of coffee.
During the COVID-19 closure, CTPH found a UK distributor so that coffee farmers could earn income without tourism.

Buyers already pay a premium for coffee from the park edge, and income from coffee does not depend on tourism. Expanding traceable shade-coffee sourcing, especially to households without tourism income, could address the livelihood gap behind poaching, though any effect on poaching has not been measured.
A 4.1 km elephant crop-raiding hotspot on the park boundary is targeted for bee fences, but past mitigation has been patchy because of limited funds and weak maintenance.
Under agreements running for over two decades, neighbouring communities may place beehives in designated zones of the park for honey collection, so beekeeping is an established local practice.
Turning bee fences into a honey business run by fence-line households could pay for the maintenance that IUCN identifies as the weak point of current mitigation.
Bee fences are mainly an elephant deterrent; they may do little against raiding by gorillas, baboons or bushpigs.

Created in 2004 to protect and manage Guinea-Bissau's biodiversity through the National System of Protected Areas, which covers about 26% of the national territory. It coordinates management of the Bijagós World Heritage property and manages the Cacheu park. Its 2006 annual report records the appointment of wardens for the Orango, João Vieira–Poilão and Cacheu parks; current park-level arrangements were not re-verified.

Conservation trust fund established in 2011 as a long-term financing mechanism for Guinea-Bissau's protected areas, with funding channelled through IBAP. It supports Orango National Park, runs the Blue Bijagós project and runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. It is listed as a member of the Consortium of African Funds for the Environment (CAFÉ).

text: Guinean NGO that supported the creation and participatory governance of the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area.

With IBAP and partners, ran a 2015–2018 initiative to conserve and restore the Cacheu mangroves, including ecological restoration of abandoned rice fields, solar salt and a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven. It reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. In Liberia's Lake Piso reserve it has supported improved stoves and a cassava processing unit under an EU-funded mangrove project.

Provided technical assistance to the coastal planning that led to the 1996 Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve. Awarded Ras Mohammed National Park IUCN Green List certification in November 2018 after an evaluation against 50 indicators.

Restoration programme uniting 10 countries and three Global Environment Facility agencies (IUCN, FAO and UNEP). Its Guinea-Bissau project works with women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River. The reviewed source does not say which agency leads the Guinea-Bissau project.

Regional coalition for the conservation and sustainable management of West Africa's coastal and marine areas. It partners with Rainforest Trust on a proposed project supporting new marine protected area designations in the Bijagós.
Raising funds, with PRCM, to support government designation of four new marine protected areas in the Bijagós, including three island community MPAs (proposed project).
National NGO supporting a network of environmental schools (EVA) around the park.

Runs a research project on the ecological integrity of the Bijagós as a key site for waders on the East Atlantic Flyway, with partners including Tiniguena. Helped develop the biodiversity and threat monitoring protocol used in Obô Natural Park of São Tomé since 2021, and a CE3C researcher reviewed the Malanza mangrove plan.
Benin's national wildlife-reserve agency; supervising administration of the Bouche du Roy marine protected area inside the reserve.
Implemented the 2013–2019 project, funded by the German International Climate Initiative, that prepared the transboundary biosphere reserve.
Worked with local partners, GIZ and both governments to create the reserve, and partners Eco-Benin on blue-carbon mangrove work.
Beninese NGO running mangrove restoration and sacralisation and a blue-carbon project in the Bouche du Roy area of the reserve.
Federal agency under the Ministry of Environment carrying out the Ogoniland clean-up, mangrove restoration and livelihood programmes, and preparing the Ramsar site management plan.
Carried out the 2011 independent environmental assessment of Ogoniland whose recommendations frame the clean-up.
Maio NGO that managed the Salinas under a 2012 delegation, monitors its birds and turtles, and leads co-management of Maio's protected areas.
National environment directorate with the mandate and authority on biodiversity and conservation in Cabo Verde.
Holds delegated management of the national-park part of the Ramsar site.
World Bank-financed coastal resilience programme; funded mangrove restoration with OIPR in Côte d'Ivoire and mangrove planting in Togo.
Management authority of the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site, mandated to enforce the law.
Ran the 2021–2023 PAPBio mangrove restoration and livelihoods project in four Keta Lagoon communities, with the Wildlife Division.
Its staff act against unsustainable logging, fishing and illegal hunting at the site; it is the implementing agency of WACA in Togo.
UNFCCC technology body that prepared a 2025 technical-assistance plan for women-led mangrove restoration and solar fish preservation in Togo's Maritime Region.
Public administrative body that manages the park under its own law (2000-024).
Conservation trust fund created in 2009 that provides long-term funding for the park, including sea surveillance and shared governance.
Named as the park's managing body in the 1993 Ramsar sheet; UNESCO names it as a partner in integrated management planning.
Senegalese marine conservation association that proposed and led the Bamboung community marine protected area project.
Community-based non-profit founded in 2007 that holds exclusive cockle and oyster use rights in Tanbi; it received the Equator Prize in 2012.
Has managed the Tanbi Wetlands Complex since 2005 and assists with enforcement under the shellfish co-management plan.
Implemented the USAID Ba Nafaa project, with WWF, that supported the Tanbi shellfish co-management plan.
Guinean NGO running mangrove restoration, solar salt, improved ovens and oyster pilots in the Konkouré delta, and a partner in the PROMAK protected-area project.
Leads the EU-funded PROMAK consortium (2025–2028) working towards legal protection of the Konkouré mangroves.
Named as the future manager of the protected area proposed for the Konkouré mangroves.
Statutory protected-area authority; carries out enforcement against encroachment at the estuary, though its mandate over wetlands is limited.
Runs mangrove planting in Freetown coastal communities under its #FreetownTheTreeTown campaign.
Ran bird-conservation and nature-guiding training around the Targreen wetland in 2024.
National authority for conservation forestry; lists the Lake Piso Multiple Sustainable Use Reserve among Liberia's protected areas.
Named in the 2007 Ramsar sheet as the agency responsible for the Lake Piso wetland.
Grantee of a 2016–2017 GEF small-grant project on sustainable fishing at Lake Piso.

Manages Iona under a long-term agreement signed in December 2019 with the Angolan environment ministry and the national biodiversity institute, covering law enforcement, wildlife monitoring, giraffe reintroductions and community programmes.
Angola's national biodiversity and protected-area institute; government signatory of the management agreement and partner of the park's funder.

Funds Iona as a 'legacy landscape', with African Parks as implementing partner and the national biodiversity institute as government partner; had an environmental and social due diligence carried out (2021–2022) and contracted the consultants for the 2025 milestone review.

Partnered in setting up a community agricultural association in Monte Negro, near Iona. Leads the Sustainable Wildlife Management Programme (EU- and AFD-funded), which works with the Kyaramacan Association in Bwabwata National Park on legal and sustainable devil's claw harvesting.
Leads oversight of the World Heritage property, coordinates the management plan from Maun, and submitted the 2024 State of Conservation report.
Runs anti-poaching patrols in the property and manages human–elephant conflict through its Problem Animal Control Unit (patrols, crop-damage compensation, farmer training).
Controls the invasive Salvinia in the property with a biological control weevil (Cyrtobagous salviniae).
Angola–Botswana–Namibia basin commission that led the Strategic Environmental Assessment of the Cubango-Okavango basin and funded climate-smart farming projects in the buffer zone.
Botswana NGO based in Maun that helped the State Party identify wildlife corridors in the eastern panhandle and works with farmers on reducing elephant conflict.

Responsible for nature conservation and protected-area management in Egypt, including Ras Mohammed; a 2023 study of the park lists its measures, such as mooring buoys, walkways, a USD 5 daily user fee and a reef-damage fee.

GEF implementing agency for the 2010–2020 protected-area financing project and for the Green Sharm El Sheikh project (approved 2022), which supports improved management of Ras Mohamed. With the Global Environment Facility, funds a Gorongosa Restoration Project programme covering park law enforcement and small grants managed by Community Natural Resources Committees.

Funded the 2010–2020 project that supported efforts to reduce tourism impacts on Ras Mohammed's reefs, coral monitoring in South Sinai and a new permit and concession system for protected areas, and funds the Green Sharm El Sheikh project.
Gabon's national parks agency: manages Akanda National Park, carries out awareness, surveillance and control missions there, and co-compiled the 2024 Ramsar sheet.
France's development agency; from 2012 to 2018 it supported ANPN's integrated management of the protected areas around Libreville, including Akanda, and co-funded the 2023 fish study.
Researchers and technicians of its hydrobiology and ichthyology laboratory carried out the 2017–2018 fish survey of the park's mangroves.
Gave technical assistance to ANPN in preparing the 2014–2018 management plan and contributed to the 2023 fish study.

A locally registered NGO, established with Gregory C. Carr's foundation, that co-manages Gorongosa National Park with the Government of Mozambique and runs its conservation, science and buffer-zone development programmes.

Mozambique's national conservation areas authority; it commissioned the 2015 external evaluation of the park's long-term co-management agreement, and the co-manager reports close coordination with it.
Holds legal authority over Bwabwata National Park, wrote its 2020/21–2029/30 management plan, and administers the hunting concessions that benefit the Kyaramacan Association.
Residents' association inside the park that represents residents, employs community game guards and resource monitors, runs the N//goabaca campsite and receives hunting-concession revenue.
Helped establish the Kyaramacan Association in 2005 and, according to the management plan, is the NGO that works most with park residents.
Signed a 2017 co-management memorandum for the protected areas, led EU ECOFAC 6 support to the natural parks, helped set up threat monitoring, and rehabilitated the park headquarters at Bom Sucesso.
Government forestry and biodiversity directorate that oversees the park; its agents carry out the park's twice-yearly biodiversity and threat monitoring.
Prepared the 2020–2025 management plans for the park's Malanza and Praia das Conchas mangroves for the park department, with CEPF funding.
Eco-guide association whose members maintain the park's trails and join its biodiversity and threat monitoring.
Manages Mafia Island Marine Park under the Board of Trustees for Marine Parks and Reserves and carries out the park's coral reef and fish monitoring.
Funds reef and fish monitoring in the park through the Blue Action Fund-supported RUMAKI-BAF project to strengthen marine protected area management in Rufiji, Mafia and Kilwa.
Runs coral restoration trials in the park and leads the CEPF-funded Kitutia Reef restoration project with Jibondo, Chole and the park authority.
Funds the 2025–2026 community coral restoration project on Kitutia Reef (grant 116131).
Its conservation officers patrol beaches in the Rufiji–Mafia Seascape to monitor sea turtle nesting, and it runs marine conservation outreach in Mafia District villages.
Manages Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, including law enforcement, gorilla tourism rules and revenue sharing with neighbouring communities.
Runs community health and livelihood programmes around Bwindi, including the Gorilla Conservation Coffee social enterprise and emergency food support during the COVID-19 closure.

A coalition of Conservation International, Fauna & Flora International and WWF that works with UWA at Bwindi, supports, with UWA and CTPH, the HUGO volunteers who herd gorillas from community land back to the park, and monitors road projects affecting it.
Supports community-level interventions outside the park and provides income to community projects.
Leads research and monitoring in the park.
